explanation.text:
(Pro. 27:1-27)

Do not confide implicitly in your plans (Pro 16:9; Pro 19:21; Jam 4:13-15).

bsb.text: Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring.

explanation.text: Avoid self-praise.

bsb.text: Let another praise you, and not your own mouth—a stranger, and not your own lips.

explanation.text:
heavy--The literal sense of "heavy," applied to material subjects, illustrates its figurative, "grievous," applied to moral.

a fool's wrath--is unreasonable and excessive.

bsb.text: A stone is heavy and sand is a burden, but aggravation from a fool outweighs them both.

explanation.text: envy--or, "jealousy" (compare Margin; Pro 6:34), is more unappeasable than the simpler bad passions.

bsb.text: Wrath is cruel and anger is like a flood, but who can withstand jealousy?

explanation.text: secret love--not manifested in acts is useless; and even, if its exhibition by rebukes wounds us, such love is preferable to the frequent (compare Margin), and hence deceitful, kisses of an enemy.

bsb.text: Better an open rebuke than love that is concealed.
The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.

explanation.text: The luxury of wealth confers less happiness than the healthy appetite of labor.

bsb.text: The soul that is full loathes honey, but to a hungry soul, any bitter thing is sweet.

explanation.text: Such are not only out of place, but out of duty and in danger.

bsb.text: Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who wanders from his home.

explanation.text:
rejoice the heart--the organ of perceiving what pleases the senses.

sweetness . . . counsel--or, "wise counsel is also pleasing."

bsb.text: Oil and incense bring joy to the heart, and the counsel of a friend is sweetness to the soul.

explanation.text: Adhere to tried friends. The ties of blood may be less reliable than those of genuine friendship.

bsb.text: Do not forsake your friend or your father’s friend, and do not go to your brother’s house in the day of your calamity; better a neighbor nearby than a brother far away.

explanation.text: The wisdom of children both reflects credit on parents and contributes to their aid in difficulties.

bsb.text: Be wise, my son, and bring joy to my heart, so that I can answer him who taunts me.

explanation.text: (Compare Pro 20:16; Pro 22:3).

bsb.text: The prudent see danger and take cover, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty.

explanation.text: Take his garment that is surety for a stranger, and take a pledge of him for a strange woman. See Gill on Proverbs 20:16, where the same proverb is, and is expressed in the same words as here.

bsb.text: Take the garment of him who posts security for a stranger; get collateral if it is for a foreigner.

explanation.text: Excessive zeal in praising raises suspicions of selfishness.

bsb.text: If one blesses his neighbor with a loud voice early in the morning, it will be counted to him as a curse.

explanation.text:
(Compare Pro 19:13).

very . . . day--literally, "a day of showers."

bsb.text: A constant dripping on a rainy day and a contentious woman are alike—

explanation.text:
hideth--or, "restrains" (that is, tries to do it); is as fruitless an effort, as that of holding the wind.

the ointment of his right hand--the organ of power (Psa 17:7; Psa 18:35). His right hand endeavors to repress perfume, but vainly. Some prefer: "His right hand comes on oil," that is, "cannot take hold." Such a woman cannot be tamed.

bsb.text: restraining her is like holding back the wind or grasping oil with one’s right hand.

explanation.text: a man sharpeneth . . . friend--that is, conversation promotes intelligence, which the face exhibits.

bsb.text: As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another.

explanation.text: Diligence secures a reward, even for the humble servant.

bsb.text: Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who looks after his master will be honored.

explanation.text: We may see our characters in the developed tempers of others.

bsb.text: As water reflects the face, so the heart reflects the true man.

explanation.text: Men's cupidity is as insatiable as the grave.

bsb.text: Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied; so the eyes of man are never satisfied.

explanation.text:
Praise tests character.

a man to his praise--according to his praise, as he bears it. Thus vain men seek it, weak men are inflated by it, wise men disregard it, etc.

bsb.text: A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but a man is tested by the praise accorded him.

explanation.text: The obstinate wickedness of such is incurable by the heaviest inflictions.

bsb.text: Though you grind a fool like grain with mortar and a pestle, yet his folly will not depart from him.

explanation.text: flocks--constituted the staple of wealth. It is only by care and diligence that the most solid possessions can be perpetuated (Pro 23:5).

bsb.text: Be sure to know the state of your flocks, and pay close attention to your herds;

explanation.text:
For riches are not for ever,.... A man cannot be assured of the continuance of them; they are uncertain things, here today and gone tomorrow: wherefore, though a man has a considerable share of them, yet should follow one calling or another; particularly husbandry is recommended, or keeping sheep and cattle, which are increasing; by which means his substance will be continued and augmented, which otherwise is not to be depended on, but in a diligent attendance to business;

and doth the crown endure to every generation? the royal crown, that is not to be depended upon; a king that wears a crown is not sure he shall always wear it, or that it shall be continued to his family one generation after another. And it is suggested, that it is not even beneath such persons to have a regard to their flocks and herds, and the increase of their riches in this way: the Chinese kings, many of them, formerly employed themselves in husbandry, and set examples of industry and diligence to their subjects; King Hezekiah provided himself possessions of flocks and herds in abundance, 2 Chronicles 32:28.

bsb.text: for riches are not forever, nor does a crown endure to every generation.

explanation.text:
The fact that providential arrangements furnish the means of competence to those who properly use them is another motive to diligence (compare Psa 65:9-13).

The hay appeareth--literally, "Grass appeareth" (Job 40:15; Psa 104:14).

bsb.text: When hay is removed and new growth appears and the grass from the hills is gathered,

explanation.text:
The lambs are for thy clothing,.... This is another argument, exciting to diligence in the pastoral calling, taken from the profit arising from it: the wool of the lambs, or rather "sheep", as many versions render it; of it cloth is made, and of that garments to be worn, to keep decent, warm, and comfortable; see Job 31:20;

and the goats are the price of thy field: these, being brought up and sold, furnish the husbandman with money to purchase more fields to feed his cattle on. The Targum is,

"the goats are for negotiation;''

with the price of them a man may purchase any of the necessaries of life for himself and family; these are negotiated, Ezekiel 27:21; the Syriac version is, "the goats are for thy food"; and so, between both the sheep and goats, man has both food and raiment; though his food is particularly mentioned in Proverbs 27:27.

bsb.text: the lambs will provide you with clothing, and the goats with the price of a field.

explanation.text:
household--literally, "house," the family (Act 16:15; Co1 1:16).

Next: Proverbs Chapter 28

bsb.text: You will have plenty of goats’ milk to feed you—food for your household and nourishment for your maidservants.
